questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are non-tender and rubbery. Dark-field microscopy of the exudate shows motile spirochetes. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) is caused by Treponema pallidum. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose is the first-line treatment. Doxycycline is used in penicillin-allergic patients for 14 days.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk with a thickened greater auricular nerve. Slit skin smear is negative. Skin biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytic infiltration and no bacilli. What is the leprosy classification?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT): few well-defined anaesthetic hypopigmented patches, thickened nerves, negative SSS, and skin biopsy showing well-formed epithelioid granulomas with no AFB. This is the paucibacillary pole of the spectrum.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompromised male develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the right T5 dermatome with severe burning pain. Which antiviral regimen is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) in an immunocompromised host requires Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day for 7-10 days. Lower doses (200 mg) are used for HSV. Valacyclovir 1 g TDS for 7 days is an alternative.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male develops tense bullae on normal and perilesional skin. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP): tense bullae on normal/perilesional skin, DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ (hemidesmosomes/BP180 antigen). Pemphigus vulgaris shows flaccid bullae with intraepidermal IgG deposition (intercellular).

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic female presents with a painful, rapidly enlarging skin lesion on the lower leg with central necrosis and surrounding violaceous border. Cultures grow mixed anaerobes and streptococci. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection involving fascia with necrosis. It is common in diabetics, shows mixed flora (Streptococcus, anaerobes), and requires immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive male (CD4 count 80 cells/uL) presents with whitish plaques on the oral mucosa that can be scraped off. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: Oral candidiasis (thrush) in immunocompromised patients is caused by Candida albicans. Whitish plaques that can be scraped off (unlike oral hairy leukoplakia), KOH showing pseudohyphae and budding yeast confirm the diagnosis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old female with known SLE develops a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash across the malar area sparing the nasolabial folds, with photosensitivity. ANA is 1:640 (speckled pattern). Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though sensitivity is low (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is highly specific and correlates with disease activity. Anti-histone is characteristic of drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with well-demarcated silvery scaly plaques on the extensor surface of elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. Which cells are primarily responsible for the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.exp: Psoriasis is driven by Th1 (IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha) and Th17 (IL-17, IL-22) lymphocytes that stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and neutrophil recruitment. The IL-23/Th17 axis is a key therapeutic target (biologics like secukinumab, ixekizumab).

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The child's sibling has similar lesions. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (cocci in clusters). Honey-yellow crusts are typical. Treatment: topical mupirocin or fusidic acid; systemic antibiotics for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female presents with flaccid bullae and erosions involving the oral mucosa and skin. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposition in the epidermis in a chicken-wire pattern. Target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris involves autoantibodies against Desmoglein 3 (primarily mucosal) and sometimes Desmoglein 1 (skin). Flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, intraepidermal acantholysis. BP180 is the target in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasias on the nose that has been slowly growing for 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) presents as a pearly papule/nodule with rolled edges, telangiectasias, on sun-exposed skin in the elderly. It is the most common skin cancer. Rarely metastasizes but is locally invasive. Squamous cell carcinoma presents as a keratotic indurated plaque.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male with chronic plaque psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Which monitoring is mandatory at a cumulative dose of 1.5 g?
questions.exp: Methotrexate (MTX) is hepatotoxic. Liver biopsy is recommended when cumulative dose reaches 1.5 g (or after every 1-1.5 g thereafter) to assess for fibrosis/cirrhosis. LFTs, CBC, and renal function should be monitored regularly. Procollagen III peptide (PIIIP) is a non-invasive alternative marker.

questions.q: A 20-year-old female presents with multiple soft, skin-colored pedunculated papules in the axilla and groin that are painless. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acrochordons (skin tags/fibroepithelial polyps) are soft, pedunculated, skin-colored papules commonly found in intertriginous areas (axilla, groin, neck). They are benign and associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome. Treatment: snipping, cryotherapy, or electrodesiccation.

questions.q: A 18-year-old male develops grouped pruritic vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillary tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposition at the DEJ. Associated systemic condition is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease). DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillary tips. Treatment: dapsone for skin lesions; gluten-free diet for both skin and gut.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male presents with painless ulcerations on the sole of the foot with destruction of underlying bone on X-ray. He has had leprosy for 8 years. What is the primary mechanism of these foot ulcers?
opts: Loss of pain and temperature sensation due to nerve damage
questions.exp: Plantar ulcers (trophic ulcers) in leprosy result from loss of protective pain sensation due to peripheral nerve damage (anaesthesia). Repeated unnoticed trauma leads to tissue breakdown and secondary infection. Not primarily vascular in origin.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with extensive perifollicular hyperkeratosis and coiled buried hairs on the thighs and upper arms. Multiple siblings have similar findings. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.exp: Keratosis pilaris (KP) shows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance. It presents with follicular hyperkeratotic papules most commonly on posterolateral upper arms, thighs, and cheeks. Often associated with atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female presents with diffuse hair loss with widening of the central part and preservation of the frontal hairline. Trichoscopy shows peripilar signs and hair diameter variability >20%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Female pattern hair loss (FPHL/Ludwig pattern) presents with diffuse thinning at the crown with preservation of the frontal hairline. Trichoscopy shows hair diameter variability >20% and peripilar signs. Treatment: topical minoxidil, oral anti-androgens.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with firm painless yellowish plaques on the eyelids for 6 months. Lipid profile shows total cholesterol of 320 mg/dL. What is this lesion called?
questions.exp: Xanthelasma palpebrarum are yellowish lipid deposits on the eyelids, often associated with hyperlipidemia. Histology shows foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) in the dermis. About 50% occur with normal lipids. Treatment: TCA application, laser, or surgical excision.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male with recurrent genital ulcers, oral ulcers, and uveitis is evaluated. The pathergy test is positive. What is the HLA association of this condition?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is characterized by recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, uveitis, and skin lesions. HLA-B51 is strongly associated. Pathergy test (positive papule/pustule 48h after skin prick) is characteristic. HLA-B27 is associated with ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male presents with sclerotic skin changes in the fingers (sclerodactyly), Raynaud's phenomenon, and telangiectasias. ANA shows anticentromere pattern. Pulmonary fibrosis is absent. What systemic sclerosis subtype does he have?
questions.exp: Limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc/CREST) involves skin limited to face, hands, and feet (sclerodactyly, Raynaud's), telangiectasias, calcinosis, esophageal dysmotility. Anti-centromere antibodies are characteristic. Pulmonary hypertension (not fibrosis) is the major late complication.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on an erythematous base in crops on the trunk, followed by pustules and crusts, all stages simultaneously present. The most feared complication in immunocompromised hosts is:
questions.exp: Varicella (chickenpox) in immunocompromised patients can cause varicella pneumonia (varicella pneumonitis), which is the most severe and potentially fatal complication. Multi-stage lesions simultaneously are characteristic of varicella.

questions.q: A 23-year-old male presents with multiple discrete, pearly, umbilicated papules on the trunk and genitalia. He is sexually active. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by MCV (a poxvirus). Clinically shows pearly, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules. In adults, genital lesions are sexually transmitted. In immunocompromised patients, lesions may be extensive. Cantharidin, cryotherapy, or curettage are used for treatment.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with raised erythematous plaques with central clearing and an advancing scaly border on the groin. KOH preparation shows fungal hyphae. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Tinea cruris (ringworm of groin) is caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton rubrum most common). Topical terbinafine (allylamine) for 2 weeks is highly effective. Oral therapy is reserved for extensive/resistant cases. Griseofulvin is fungistatic and requires longer courses.

questions.q: A punch biopsy of a suspicious pigmented lesion shows malignant melanocytes extending into the reticular dermis. Mitotic rate is 2/mm2. Breslow thickness is 2.8 mm. According to AJCC 8th edition, what is the T category?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition for melanoma: T3 = Breslow 2.01-4.0 mm. 'a' = no ulceration and mitotic rate <1/mm2, 'b' = ulceration present OR mitotic rate >=1/mm2. Here, Breslow 2.8 mm + mitotic rate 2/mm2 = T3b. T4 is >4 mm.

questions.q: A 24-year-old female develops erythematous oozing pruritic patches on her earlobes and wrists 48 hours after wearing new jewellery. Patch testing shows a positive reaction to nickel sulfate. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to nickel is a classic Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes. It occurs 48-72 hours after antigen exposure. Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosis.

questions.q: A neonate develops flaccid blisters and skin peeling in sheets within 48 hours of birth. The mother had Staphylococcal mastitis. Cultures of the blister fluid are sterile. What toxin is responsible?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B produced by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. Toxins cleave desmoglein 1 in the superficial epidermis. Blister fluid is sterile as toxins act at distant skin sites via hematogenous spread.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male with HIV presents with painless verrucous cauliflower-like growths on the perianal area. HPV typing shows HPV-16. What is the greatest risk associated with this HPV type at this location?
opts: Transformation to anal squamous cell carcinoma
questions.exp: HPV-16 and HPV-18 are high-risk oncogenic subtypes. Perianal HPV-16 infection in immunocompromised (HIV) patients carries significant risk of progression to anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) and invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the anus.

questions.q: A 14-year-old presents with loss of skin color in patches around the mouth, eyes, and dorsum of hands for 1 year. Wood's lamp examination shows chalky-white fluorescence with accentuation. Autoantibodies and cytotoxic T cells target which structure?
questions.exp: Vitiligo is caused by autoimmune destruction of melanocytes. Autoantibodies (and cytotoxic T cells) target melanocyte antigens including tyrosinase, TYRP1, and TYRP2. Wood's lamp accentuates depigmented areas (chalky white fluorescence).

questions.q: During a shave biopsy procedure, the surgeon cuts into the reticular dermis instead of remaining superficial. Which layer should shave biopsies ideally remain within to avoid scarring?
questions.exp: Shave biopsies should ideally remain in the papillary dermis. Extending into the reticular dermis increases the risk of hypertrophic scarring or depressed scars. They are suitable for exophytic lesions, seborrheic keratoses, and melanocytic nevi (not for suspected melanoma).

questions.q: A 28-year-old female taking oral contraceptives develops brown hyperpigmentation over the forehead, cheeks, and upper lip that worsens with sun exposure. Wood's lamp examination shows accentuation. What is the treatment of first choice?
questions.exp: Melasma (chloasma) is treated first-line with topical hydroquinone 4% (a depigmenting agent inhibiting tyrosinase) combined with strict broad-spectrum sunscreen and avoidance of triggers (OCP, UV). Kligman's formula (hydroquinone 5% + tretinoin 0.1% + fluocinolone 0.01%) is also highly effective.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male on long-term clofazimine for multibacillary leprosy develops a reddish-brown discoloration of his skin and conjunctivae. He is concerned about this side effect. What is the best explanation?
opts: Crystal deposition of clofazimine in macrophages and skin
Melanin overproduction stimulated by the drug
questions.exp: Clofazimine (a riminophenazine dye) causes reddish-brown to black skin discoloration due to crystal deposition of the drug in skin macrophages and adipose tissue. This is the major cosmetic side effect and is dose-dependent and reversible on stopping the drug. It also causes ichthyosis and GI symptoms.
